title: What I Wish I Knew Before Studying Abroad (Estonia)
format: Talking head with two angles (front + side) switching on each of 9 numbered things, 0.5 s black number cards (01-09), official pages shown as receipts
hook: These are the things I wish I knew before studying abroad, and most of them are not about your school.

record.where: Not the usual desk: the spot in the new flat with the biggest window, sitting side-on to the light, with depth behind (bookshelf, plant, sofa back or a doorway). Record the first 30 s and the winter short a second time after dark with the dark window behind and a lamp on her.

script:
### Open

These are the things I wish I knew before studying abroad, and most of them are not about your school.

*[on screen: black card "9 THINGS"]*

I moved to Tallinn, which is the capital of Estonia, in autumn 2025 for my master's degree, and I'm now in my second year.

I'll go through nine of them. One of them is how I renewed my Nigerian passport through the embassy in Sweden, and I didn't have to go to Sweden. And I'll tell you how long Estonia lets you stay after your studies end.

These are practical things based on my experience.

Emphasis on based on my experience.

I'll be using Estonia a lot as my example, but I think most of this applies regardless of the country you're going to, or at least it's good to know.

### Understand how the country runs

*[on screen: 01 / how the country runs]*

The first thing I'd tell anyone about to study abroad is to try to understand how the country they're going to runs.

So don't just be focused on your school, your programme.

Understand how things get done in the country.

In Estonia, for example, when you get here as an international student, you'll probably come on a visa.

One of the things you have to do is apply for a residence permit card.

Estonians have an ID card that everyone has, and as an international student, the residence permit card kind of works the same way.

So basically, you use it to prove who you are online, and to sign documents digitally.

You can set it up on your phone.

Banks use it, and a lot of websites here in Estonia even ask for it before you set up an account and all of that.

*[on screen: residence permit card = prove who you are online + sign documents digitally + banks and websites]*

Now, this might be different in the country you're going to, if it's not Estonia.

It might not be something as digital as that.

Things might be more manual.

So you want to know what's up.

If I come on a student visa, do I have to get the residence permit?

Or do I keep studying on my visa?

Just try to find out how it all works.

In Estonia, before your residence permit card comes, I don't even think you can start a proper job.

In Tallinn, public transport is free, but only if you're a registered Tallinn resident.

So if you're not a resident, you pay for transport.

So it influences the decisions you make in that way, and you need to understand how it works.

You also want to register your address and stuff like that.

Even if you're living in the school dormitory, you should still register that address, because you're a tenant regardless.

*[on screen: Estonia: register your address within 1 month of your permit · Tallinn: free public transport for registered Tallinn residents (as of November 2026)]*

But again, the rules can change, and every country is different.

So try to understand how the country you're going to runs, or how the city runs, and try to set things up for yourself.

Okay.

### Can you work while studying abroad?

*[on screen: 02 / work]*

Another thing to find out before you study abroad is the work situation in the country or the city you want to study in.

If you're interested in working as an international student, you need to do your research on how things work in the country you're studying in.

For example, if you're coming to Estonia to study, you can work.

According to the Police and Border Guard Board, students on residence permits for study don't need a separate work permit to work.

*[on screen: the Police and Border Guard Board line "no need for separate work permit", highlighted]*

But there are conditions attached to you working.

Even if you're working, the condition is that you have to keep studying full-time, and your work cannot get in the way of your studies.

So if you interrupt your studies, or you don't complete your programme to the required extent, then your residence permit ends 30 days after that.

*[on screen: Estonia, study residence permit: no separate work permit · keep studying full-time · studies come first]*

Also, this is another thing.

What happens after you graduate?

So if you hope to move away from the city, or maybe you hope to spend more time in the city, try to find out what the gist is.

After I graduate, how can I stay back in the country?

Do I get a work permit, and all of that?

So you have to start planning for that, or at least in a way, from the onset.

In Estonia, for example, after a residence permit for study ends, you can stay 270 more days, which is about nine months, in the country.

You can work during that time, and if you find a job, you can apply for a residence permit for work, right?

*[on screen: after your study permit ends: 270 more days (about 9 months) · doesn't apply if the permit was revoked or ended early]*

So just try to understand how it works.

### Health insurance as an international student

*[on screen: 03 / health insurance]*

Another thing you need to get right before you study abroad is health insurance as a student.

Health insurance is very important.

You don't want to be in a country or a city where you don't know so many people, where you're still trying to build a community around yourself, and you don't have health insurance.

You need that insurance.

At least from my experience, when I was coming from Nigeria, I had to buy an insurance.

It wasn't really one of those ones that cover a lot.

So yeah.

You can also try to understand how health insurance works in the country.

Is it free?

Is it subsidised for students?

In Estonia, for example, if you're a student from outside the EU, you need private health insurance.

Again, I had to buy one before I even went to apply for my visa.

If you get a job here with an employment contract, then things can change a little bit.

The employer pays social tax, and then you get state health insurance through the Estonian Health Insurance Fund, right?

*[on screen: student from outside the EU = private health insurance · employment contract = state health insurance (Tervisekassa), starting 14 days after you start work]*

But if you don't have a job that covers you, you have to get private health insurance.

So you need to put that in place, and read and understand what your private health insurance covers before you buy it.

### The weather (how dark the winter gets)

*[on screen: 04 / the weather]*

The weather.

Another thing you need to know before you study abroad is the weather.

In Estonia, for example, it can get really cold.

Winter is long.

Winter is dark.

Winter is so cold.

In Tallinn in December, you get about six hours of daylight.

*[say twice]*

*[on screen: Tallinn, December: about 6 hours of daylight]*

So try to understand how the weather works and prepare for it.

Like, really prepare for it.

I know someone here who was telling me about when they had just arrived.

In their first winter, they literally landed in the hospital.

So you want to prepare for the weather if you're coming from somewhere that is way different.

If you're coming from somewhere like Nigeria all the way to the Baltics here, it's like going from one end of the world to the other end of the world in terms of the weather.

### Finding a place to live

*[on screen: 05 / a place to live]*

Okay, that's four. The passport one is number eight, I'm getting there.

Another thing to think about before you study abroad is a place to live, and finding a place to live.

I think this is usually easy if you come as a student and your school has a dormitory, right?

I stayed in the dormitory for about a month plus, and it was really nice.

My flatmates were really nice.

But I moved out of the dormitory afterwards.

When you stay in the dormitory, of course you pay less.

Mine was about €250 a month.

But if you're someone who would like to live outside the dormitory, then you might want to roughly double that budget, right?

*[on screen: my dorm: about €250 a month · living outside it: roughly double (my experience, prices change)]*

So basically, think about what kind of living fits you, and your budget, even before you come.

It will make life easier for you.

### Learning the language

*[on screen: 06 / the language]*

If you're studying in a country where the official language is not English, you might want to consider learning the language.

Of course, you're probably studying in a programme where the language of the course is English.

But if the language of the country is not English, I think learning it helps a lot.

I was reading one of Khaled Hosseini's books, *And the Mountains Echoed*, and one of the statements that really stood out to me was this.

"If culture was a house, then language was the key to the front door, to all the rooms inside."

*[on screen: the quote + "Khaled Hosseini, And the Mountains Echoed" (hold the book up if you have it)]*

So if you really want to interact with the culture, you need to try to learn the language.

In my school this is easy, because we compulsorily have to do an Estonian A1 class.

It might not be the same in another country.

But even if it's not something that is required, I think it's always nice to interact with the culture where you're schooling through the language as well.

If you choose to spend a year, two years of your life in a place, you might as well just enjoy it.

And part of enjoying it is interacting with the culture, interacting with the language.

### Your driving licence abroad

*[on screen: 07 / your driving licence]*

Another thing to check before studying abroad is your driver's licence.

If you drive in Nigeria, you want to check if your Nigerian driver's licence can work in the country you're going to.

In Estonia, the Nigerian driver's licence is valid for 12 months from when your residency starts, and then you have to exchange it for an Estonian one.

I have exchanged mine.

Right.

*[on screen: Estonia: Nigerian licence valid 12 months from your residency start · then exchange it (generally no exams) · the old licence is handed over]*

So if driving is something you do, and you want to continue doing it while schooling, you need to understand, like, oh, what's the way to get a driver's licence in this place, and all of that.

### Renewing your Nigerian documents abroad

*[on screen: 08 / your passport from abroad]*

Another practical thing is renewing your Nigerian documents while you're not in Nigeria.

This could be any Nigerian document.

For example, your Nigerian passport.

My Nigerian passport expired some months ago, and I had to renew it.

Obviously, I wasn't going to go to Nigeria for that.

If you're an international student in another country, and you know you won't be going home frequently, then you need to do a bit of research on how to go about renewing your documents whenever they expire.

There's no Nigerian embassy in Estonia here, so I had to renew mine through the Nigerian Embassy in Stockholm, in Sweden.

And the Nigerian government has launched a contactless passport renewal option for eligible Nigerians in Europe, which is the option that I used.

So I did it in Sweden, and I didn't have to go to Sweden to do it.

### Enjoy it

*[on screen: card linking to the passport renewal video (kit 02) + the Ministry of Interior page as a receipt]*

*[on screen: 09 / enjoy it]*

Also, last but not the least, if you're schooling abroad, you also want to try to enjoy living there.

Be open-minded to enjoying things there.

There are things you would not like, and there are things you will like.

But be more open-minded to just enjoying the things that you like.

Even though you're going to be there for a short time, even if it's just for the duration of your study, and you're going to go back, you want to just enjoy the place as well.

Go for Erasmus programmes.

I've been on two Erasmus programmes so far.

Join different programmes in school, you know, meet people, enjoy it.

It's a new country, a new city.

I know that studying abroad, it will literally take your whole life if you give it, especially if you're working.

But just try to breathe the air of the country a little bit.

Okay.

*[outro: record both, we use the one that fits]*

A: And if you're Nigerian and your passport is going to expire while you're abroad, I made a whole video on how I renewed mine from Estonia, step by step. It's right here.

B: And if you're from Nigeria and you're thinking about studying in Europe, watch the video I made on what nobody warned me about studying in Europe as a Nigerian. It's right here.

script:
### Open

*[on screen: title box "COST OF STUDYING IN ESTONIA (NON-EU)". Passport + calculator in her hands. The receipt strip starts printing on the right.]*

How much does it really cost to study in Estonia if you're coming from Nigeria, or from anywhere outside the EU?

I get this question a lot, every time I post a video.

So I've gone through every cost, from the 100 euros you pay just to apply, all the way to the African store.

One of these schools wants your whole first year's tuition before your acceptance is even final.

And there's one amount you have to show in your bank account before you get your visa, and it's not your tuition.

Every number is from an official page as I'm recording this, and I'm putting all the links in the description box.

And a lot of it is also from my own experience.

I think the cost of living in Estonia is a little bit expensive compared to other European countries I've been to.

So let's start with the first cost.

### The application fee

The first cost of studying in Estonia is, of course, the application fee, because you need to apply, right?

There are some major universities here in Estonia, like Tallinn University, the University of Tartu and TalTech.

At all three of them, the application fee for international students is 100 euros.

*[on screen: application fee = €100 per university (Tallinn University, University of Tartu, TalTech). RECEIPT LINE 01.]*

And that 100 euros is for one university.

At each of these schools, paying it once lets you apply to two programmes at that school.

So if you apply to two different universities, you pay two application fees.

Think of it more as a form fee.

You pay it to be considered, and you don't get it back if you don't get admitted.

So pick your two programmes well before you pay.

That's the small one. The next one is where the real money is.

### Tuition fees in Estonia for non-EU students

Tuition is where the real money is when you study in Estonia.

For students from outside the EU, tuition depends on the university and on the programme, right?

At Tallinn University, master's programmes starting in 2027 cost about 4,000 to 7,000 euros a year.

*[on screen: Tallinn University fee page, master's starting 2027/2028: €4,000 to €7,000 a year. RECEIPT LINE 02.]*

A few programmes charge students from outside the EU more.

My programme, Human-Computer Interaction, is one of them.

And I'm just realising that even my programme's fee has increased since I came in.

I paid 6,000 euros a year, and now it's 7,000 euros a year for non-EU students.

*[on screen: the real TLU table, HCI row highlighted: €7,000 a year non-EU / €4,000 a year EU (2027/2028). "€6,000" crossed out beside it.]*

So you have to check the page for your programme.

And the University of Tartu shows you how much it can change from one programme to another.

At the University of Tartu, for example, International Relations is 4,800 euros a year for non-EU students, as I'm recording this video.

Software Engineering is 7,200 euros a year.

And Analytical Chemistry is 9,000 euros a year.

*[on screen: University of Tartu, per year, non-EU: International Relations €4,800 / Software Engineering €7,200 / Analytical Chemistry €9,000]*

So again, it depends on the programme.

Check the page for your exact programme and your exact intake year, because the same school can charge two programmes very differently.

### When you have to pay your tuition

And how early you pay can change your plans as much as how much you pay.

When you're coming to Estonia as a non-EU student, you usually pay part of your tuition before you even arrive.

How much you pay first depends on the school.

I paid for my first semester before coming in.

At Tallinn University, you pay the first semester's fee to finalise your acceptance.

At the University of Tartu, you pre-pay half of the first semester's fee after you get your admission decision.

And Tartu sends your official admission letter for the visa only after they receive that payment.

And this is the school I told you about at the start.

At TalTech, you pay the full first year, so two semesters, before your acceptance is final.

*[on screen: pay before you arrive / Tallinn University = 1st semester / University of Tartu = half of the 1st semester / TalTech = the full 1st year]*

*[optional, only if you agree, question 5]*
And if you're paying from a Nigerian bank, the Central Bank of Nigeria raised the limit for school fees abroad to 25,000 dollars a semester in June 2026.

I'll add the links to all of these, so you can get the updated information for your intake.

### Visa and residence permit fees

The next money you spend to study in Estonia is for your visa and your residence permit.

If you're a non-EU student, you apply for your visa first, because that's what gets you into the country.

It's called a D visa, and it's a long-stay visa.

The residence permit comes later, after you arrive in Estonia.

The D visa fee is 120 euros.

When you get to Estonia, you apply for your residence permit for study, and the state fee for that is 225 euros.

*[on screen: D visa = €120 / residence permit for study = €225 when you apply in Estonia (Police and Border Guard Board student guide, 9 July 2026). RECEIPT LINES 03 + 04.]*

And if there's no Estonian embassy in the country you're applying from, you have to travel to where you can apply.

For example, in my case, I went to Cairo to apply for my visa.

So add that trip to your budget.

You'll pay for flights, for a hotel or an Airbnb, and then for your flight down to Tallinn.

### Proof of funds for studying in Estonia

And this is the amount I said you have to show before you get your visa.

Proof of funds is the money you have to show you have when you apply to study in Estonia.

I needed my proof of funds for my visa.

As of 2026, the Police and Border Guard Board's student guide says 880 euros per month.

*[on screen: the police student guide (9 July 2026), "880 euros per month per applicant" highlighted. RECEIPT LINE 05: €880 × months (to show).]*

That number is four times the subsistence level, which is set every year, so it can change.

For the D visa, the guide asks for bank statements from the three months before you apply.

And for the residence permit, you need to have that 880 euros a month for the whole time your permit is valid.

I can't fully remember, but I think I showed a full year when I applied.

So there's always a fee per month, and you multiply it by however many months is required at the time.

Check with the embassy where you're applying, so you know what they want from you.

And have your proof of funds ready even before you apply, because you don't want to be scrambling for your bank statement, right?

### Health insurance for students in Estonia

Health insurance is the cost people don't usually budget for when they plan to study in Estonia.

If you're from outside the EU, you need health insurance to even apply for your visa.

The police guide says it has to cover your whole stay, and for the residence permit, the whole time your permit is valid.

Tallinn University says you need internationally valid private health insurance.

*[on screen: private health insurance, valid internationally, for your whole stay and permit. RECEIPT LINE 06.]*

I didn't get a very expensive one.

Mine didn't even cost me up to 50,000 naira.

But to be honest, it didn't cover so much. It was mainly for the visa.

Someone I know used a provider called Swisscare, and they were able to use theirs a lot more.

So you want to get a solid provider.

Get quotes from a few of them and compare.

And this next bit is how it works when you actually get sick here.

If you're using private insurance while you live here, what usually happens is that you pay at the hospital first, and then you claim your money back from your insurance.

So read well what your policy covers, and make sure it doesn't run out.

When you first arrive as a student, you're using private insurance.

If you start working in Estonia, you can then get health insurance through work.

### Rent in Tallinn as a student

*[prop: your keys]*

Rent is the next cost of studying in Estonia, and I'm talking about Tallinn here.

Tallinn University has dormitories, and they're very affordable.

A place in the dorm is about 250 euros a month, and that already includes utilities.

Utilities are your bills, like heating, water and electricity.

*[on screen: Tallinn University dorm = about €250 a month, utilities included / private flat €400 to €900 a month + utilities (€80-150 in summer, €120-250 in winter) (Tallinn University). RECEIPT LINE 07.]*

If you want to live outside the dorm, you'd probably have to double that budget, because you're paying your utilities separately and all of that.

For a private flat, if you don't mind staying somewhere small, I'd say a budget of 500 euros minimum can still work.

Tallinn University's own page puts private flats at 400 to 900 euros a month, plus utilities.

I stayed in the dorm for about a month before I moved out.

It was really nice, and the dorm is not so bad. You have flatmates and all of that.

Living outside the dorm, my budget was roughly double.

And when you move out, you pay a deposit and all of that.

Even in the dorm, you actually pay a deposit.

So if you're thinking about money and you're on a tight budget, I would absolutely advise staying in the dorm.

Or sharing.

A few people I know just came in, and they rented an apartment together and are sharing the flat, and that also makes it affordable.

### Transport costs in Tallinn and Tartu

Transport is another cost of studying in Estonia, and again, I'm talking more about Tallinn than Tartu.

Public transport in Tallinn is free once you get your residence permit and you're registered as a Tallinn resident.

Without that, you have to pay.

When I came in, I didn't have my residence permit for about a month, and I was paying an average of around 30 euros a month for transport.

*[on screen: Tallinn = free for registered residents / before that: 30-day ticket €30, one-hour ticket €2 (Visit Tallinn, May 2026). RECEIPT LINE 08.]*

Once you get your residence permit, you don't have to pay any more.

Tartu is different.

People I know who've lived in Tartu say it's much cheaper to live in, because Tallinn is the capital city.

In Tartu, I don't think transport is free, but the tickets are affordable.

The University of Tartu says a monthly card is about 13 euros if you're under 26, and it can be less with a student card.

*[on screen: Tartu monthly card = €12.95 under 26 (University of Tartu) / €7.67 with a student card (Study in Estonia)]*

And a lot of people cycle, of course, when it's not winter.

If you can get a bike that's not so expensive, you can cycle around too.

Two more costs, and then I'll tell you everything to put in your own budget.

### Food and phone costs in Estonia

title: Studying in Nigeria vs Europe: The Real Differences
format: TV / slide behind her (a NIGERIA | ESTONIA board per difference) + black number cards + real pages on screen
hook: There's so much difference between studying in Nigeria and studying in Europe. The 70 percent that gets you an A in Nigeria is a D on Estonia's grading scale.

record.where: Living room (or wherever the new flat has a TV or a 1.5 m plain light wall), not the usual desk; window light in front or to the side
record.how: Sitting on a stool or sofa edge on the right third, chest up, TV or empty wall filling the left 55-60 %, eye-level camera, room above the head and to the right for the 9:16 crop; turn and point at the screen at each new difference; record the first 30 s twice
record.props: A4 sheet with a big hand-written 70% (D on the back); optional Nigerian result slip (blurred) and a printed course programme
record.wear: Plain solid top, no fine stripes or checks

script:
### Open

There's so much difference between studying in Nigeria and studying in Europe.

The 70 percent that gets you an A in Nigeria is a D on Estonia's grading scale.

*[hold up the 70% card]*

I schooled in Nigeria, and now I'm doing my master's at Tallinn University in Estonia.

I feel like the educational system is just so different.

I have a video on this, "nobody warned me about studying in Europe as a Nigerian", and I thought I would do a follow-up.

Of course, there are loads of differences, and based on your own experience, you'll find different differences.

But I thought I would go over it again based on my experience here, how you're graded, deadlines and stuff like that.

Later on, I'll tell you why I gave up on my degree at LAUTECH. And at the end, what schooling in Nigeria gives you that still helps me here.

And by Europe, I mean Estonia, where I am, because I'm not schooling in all of Europe.

### The lecturer-student relationship

*[on screen: black card "01 · LECTURERS"]*

First of all, I think the lecturer-student relationship is reasonably different between Nigeria and Europe.

Respect shows up in different ways.

The way you respect your lecturers or your professors in Nigeria is very different from the way respect is done here.

In Nigeria, you do not call your lecturer by their first name.

Here in Estonia, everyone is on a first-name basis, and that includes your lecturers.

Well, that's just a small one.

The bigger one is how you're graded.

### How you're assessed

*[on screen: black card "02 · ASSESSMENT"]*

How you're assessed is also different between Nigeria and Europe, right?

In a lot of Nigerian universities, the final exam carries most of your grade.

Sometimes the final exam is 70 percent of your grade, and your continuous assessment is maybe 30 percent.

*[on screen: University of Nigeria, Nsukka (example): 30% continuous assessment + 70% exam]*

So the assignments and your tests, they matter, but the exam at the end really decides a lot of things.

And that's why most of us who school in Nigeria tend to prepare for that big exam day.

But here, it is different.

Work is spread across the whole semester, right?

So instead of the grade relying heavily on the exam, the course might be graded on a project, an essay, a presentation or group work, and that can literally be most of your grade.

Or even all of it.

Group work is such a common thing here, at least in my programme.

And in my school, the lecturer lets you know how you'll be assessed before the course even really starts.

In the first class, the lecturer walks you through the course programme, how you're going to be assessed and all of that.

So you really have to start working from week one.

Because by the final weeks, which are the exam weeks, most of your grade is already decided.

And if you're wondering what happens when you fail or miss an exam here, that's next.

### When you fail or miss an exam

*[on screen: black card "03 · EXAMS"]*

What happens when you fail or miss an exam is also different in Nigeria and in Estonia, where I am.

In a lot of Nigerian universities, if you fail a course, it becomes a carryover.

So you register for it again and write it in a later session.

At Tallinn University, where I'm schooling, it works like this.

A main exam is usually given two dates, plus one retake date.

You register for the exam yourself in the study information system, right?

And if you register and you don't show up, and you didn't cancel, you're marked "non-appeared", and you lose one attempt.

If you fail the main exam, you can retake it once, on the retake date.

And if you still don't pass, you just have to take the whole course again.

*[on screen: Tallinn University: 2 main exam dates + 1 retake date. Register yourself. Cancel at least 24 hours before. No-show without cancelling = "non-appeared", one attempt gone. Fail the retake = take the course again]*

So if you can't make it for an exam, cancel your registration before the deadline, which is 24 hours before the exam, so you don't lose that attempt.

### Grading: Nigerian CGPA vs Estonian A to F

*[on screen: black card "04 · GRADES"]*

Grading is another big difference between Nigeria and Europe, because the two systems look alike, but they work differently.

Remember the 70 percent from the start? This is where it comes from.

In Nigeria, most universities use a five-point scale.

A is 5 points, B is 4 points, and it goes down from there.

All your grades add up to your CGPA, and your CGPA decides your class of degree.

First class is 4.5 and above, second class upper is 3.5 and above, and all of that.

*[on screen: Nigeria (UNN example): A = 70 to 100 = 5 points. First class = CGPA 4.50 and above. Second class upper = 3.50 and above]*

In Estonia, you also get a letter. A, B, C, D, E or F.

And each letter has a number. A is 5, B is 4, and downward like that.

So far, it sounds the same.

The difference is what it takes to get each letter.

In Nigeria, an A usually starts at 70.

In Estonia, the education agency, Harno, lists an A as 91 to 100 percent.

So with 70, you don't get an A. On that scale, 70 is a D.

And at my school, each course also sets out its own criteria for each grade, so read them.

*[on screen: Harno's scale: A 91-100%, B 81-90%, C 71-80%, D 61-70%, E 51-60%, F 0-50% (fail)]*

And some courses here don't even get a grade. They're just pass or fail.

I'm not sure pass or fail courses are that popular in Nigeria.

But here, pass or fail courses are very normal.

I don't think there's been a semester that I didn't have a pass or fail course.

### Credits and ECTS

*[on screen: black card "05 · CREDITS"]*

Credits are another thing that works differently between Nigeria and Europe.

Your CGPA in Nigeria is weighted by credit units.

Your average here is weighted by credits too.

And the credits here have a name you see everywhere when you're schooling in Europe.

They're called ECTS.

The European Credit Transfer and Accumulation System is how universities across Europe count your work, so your credits can move between countries.

For example, I did two Erasmus programmes, one in Portugal and one in Cyprus.

The credits I got from those short programmes, I was able to transfer back to my university.

And there's also the time system, right?

A full-time year is 60 ECTS.

In Estonia, one credit is 26 hours of work, and that includes classes, reading and assignments.

So a six-credit course is about 156 hours of work, right?

*[on screen: 1 ECTS in Estonia = 26 hours. 6 ECTS = about 156 hours. 60 ECTS = one full-time year]*

And most of those hours are not in a classroom, which changes what class feels like.

### The classroom and independent study

*[on screen: black card "06 · CLASS"]*

Another difference between studying in Nigeria and Europe is the classroom setup.

In a lot of Nigerian universities, especially in the big general courses, classes can be very large, and the lecturer does most of the talking.

You listen, you take notes, and you read those notes for the exam.

Here, as far as I can see, the classes are smaller, and you're also expected to participate.

And then there's something called independent study.

In Estonia, one credit is 26 hours of your work, and most of those hours are not in a classroom.

They are on you.

So nobody checks if you did the reading.

You just find out yourself.

It shows in the way you understand the course, the way you discuss, and all of that.

### School life online

*[on screen: black card "07 · ONLINE"]*

Studying in Europe also means a lot of your school life happens online.

You still go to class, but so many things are online, and there isn't much submitting on paper or anything like that.

For example, at Tallinn University, we have some systems that we use.

We have the study information system, everybody calls it ÕIS, where you register for your courses and your exams, and you see your results.

You also have Moodle, where your course can happen.

I think most of the lecturers in my programme prefer Google Classroom.

And there are standards.

Even when you're writing your thesis, there are standards in terms of deadlines on the side of students, and there are standards on the side of the lecturers too.

For example, lecturers have seven days to put exam results in the system, or ten days if more than 50 students registered.

*[on screen: Tallinn University: results in the system within 7 days (10 days if more than 50 students registered). Contest a result within 10 working days]*

So you don't have to anticipate or guess. Things are standardised on both sides, the student side and the lecturer side.

When your results come out, you can get feedback.

In fact, you can even contest your grade if you have enough evidence, and you have 10 working days to do that.

In Nigeria, a lot of universities also have online portals, so all of this won't be new to you if you move abroad.

The basic thing is, as a student, turn on the notifications for all those systems.

Google Classroom, Moodle, this and that, turn on the notifications.

And in a bit, I'll tell you why I gave up on my degree at LAUTECH.

### Campus life

*[on screen: black card "08 · CAMPUS"]*

Campus life, I feel like campus life is very different between Nigeria and Europe.

Maybe it's because I'm doing my master's and not a bachelor's.

But I feel like in Nigeria, a lot of your life is just embedded in campus, because your university is big, and usually far from where you live, or far from the city.

A lot of Nigerian universities are kind of like small towns.

There's the hostel, there are markets, there's a church, there are so many things inside.

Even getting from your hostel to your faculty may mean taking a shuttle inside the university.

But here, it is different.

My university is right here in the city centre, so it's a normal city commute.

Because the campus is not as huge, the city is where student life happens.

And it's even more different at master's level, because you probably have work and all of that.

What I would just say is that your social life won't come to you the way it does on a Nigerian campus.

On a Nigerian campus, you get entangled in social life automatically, because you find yourself there.

Here, you have to go out and find your social life yourself, in your class, at student events, in the city and all of that.

### Strikes and the academic calendar

*[on screen: black card "09 · STRIKES"]*

Another big difference between Nigeria and Europe is how predictable the academic calendar is.

If you've been to a Nigerian public university, you know about ASUU strikes.

ASUU is the union for university lecturers, and in 2022, their national strike lasted eight months, from February to October.

*[optional, only if you say yes to question 5]*
And in August this year, ASUU branches at about 20 state universities went on strike again over unpaid salaries.

I used to be a student of LAUTECH, Ladoke Akintola University of Technology in Ogbomoso.

And the strikes were one of the reasons why I gave up on pursuing my degree at LAUTECH.

It felt like it was always on strike.

And it wasn't only the national ASUU strikes. LAUTECH was owned by two states, Oyo and Osun, and when the money ran short, the lecturers there went on strike over unpaid salaries.

Between 2016 and 2018, the school was shut or on strike for months at a time.

*[on screen: LAUTECH: jointly owned by Oyo and Osun states until 2020. Shut for long stretches in 2016 and 2017, another long strike in 2018 (BellaNaija, The Will, ICIR)]*

Of course, lecturers aren't intentionally being wicked.

With strikes, they are fighting for their own pay and for funding.

As much as Nigerian students complain about learning in hard conditions, I think a lot of Nigerian lecturers also teach in really hard conditions.

It goes both ways.

So the academic calendar in Nigeria might not be as reliable.

Here, the academic calendar is published ahead of time.

At my school, this year's calendar was approved in March, almost five months before the semester started in August.

So you can plan your year around it. You plan your job, you plan your travel, you plan your holiday.

So if you're here, you want to take advantage of this as much as you can.

Plan your thesis, plan your internship, plan your job search.

This is a good advantage.

### What a Nigerian education gives you

I also think that schooling in Nigeria, and I've said this in a video before, gives you so much advantage if you use it well.

They are two different systems, but there's a lot of advantage you can get if you schooled in Nigeria before.

A lot of us that had our foundational education in Nigeria are good at handling a lot of material under pressure.

It's what our exams trained us to do.

And I think we are resourceful. If something is not working, we find another way, right?

And if you're here, that habit also helps.

I think the respect we're raised with still works here. It just shows in a different way.

For example, being respectful to your lecturer here might look like being prepared, keeping your deadlines and all of that.

Starting your work early, asking for help.

You can ask for help. You can really ask for help.

So if you studied in Nigeria and you're moving to Europe to study, you already have a lot of advantages that you're bringing in from Nigeria.

I can guarantee you that you have a lot, if you don't throw them away.

Don't treat your education from Nigeria as something you just forget about.

I promise you, it's gonna help you if you know how to use it well.

If you schooled in Nigeria, tell me in the comments which of these differences you'd find hardest.

- A: "If your first degree is in something different from what you want to study now, I made a video on getting into a master's when your degree is unrelated, and how to switch. It's right here."
- B: "And if you haven't watched 'nobody warned me about studying in Europe as a Nigerian', that's the one I made before this one, on the things that surprised me when I first came. It's right here."

script:
### Can you do a master's in a different field?

*[setup 2 for this part, then Setup 1]*

Can you do a master's in a different field from your bachelor's degree?

I do not have a computer science degree.

I have a bachelor's degree in chemistry, and right now I have a career as a full stack developer, and I'm also currently doing my master's in human-computer interaction.

And I also got into a computer science master's without a computer science bachelor's, and I'll tell you how.

If you think that your degree, your bachelor's degree, has locked you out of switching fields when you want to transition, then this video is for you.

*[only if posting before 1 March 2027]*
Applications for my own programme for 2027 opened on the 1st of November, so if you're applying this year, this is the time to read this properly.

I'll show you how switching careers works, through master's, through jobs, or both, and I'll use my own path as the example all the way through. And at the end, the four questions your motivation letter has to answer when you're switching.

### Read the admission requirements properly

*[on screen: the three groups, then the Copenhagen page, then the TLU page]*

If you want to do a master's in a different field from your bachelor's, the admission requirements page decides a lot of things, so you have to read it properly.

From what I have seen, programmes usually fall into three groups.

There are some programmes that take any bachelor's degree, like the conversion courses in the UK.

There are some that ask for a degree or experience in the field.

And there are some that ask for specific courses on your transcript.

*[on screen: 1. any bachelor's degree / 2. a degree OR experience in the field / 3. specific courses on your transcript]*

The third group is where a lot of people get caught.

Let's take the computer science master's degree at the University of Copenhagen as an example.

If your bachelor's is from another university, their page asks for at least 60 ECTS of computer science courses, including programming, computer systems architecture, and theoretical computer science.

It also asks for at least 7.5 ECTS of maths.

If you don't know what ECTS means, they're the study credits used in Europe. A full-time year of study is usually worth 60 of them.

So when they say a related field can apply, it means a related field that has a year's worth of computer science already on your transcript.

*[on screen: the Copenhagen page on the TV, "60 ECTS" and "7.5 ECTS" in yellow marker]*

That's a strict door for someone like me.

*[say twice]*

But on the same page, they say they can also admit people whose educational qualifications are judged equivalent after an individual assessment.

And if your desired field is very far away from what you did your bachelor's degree in, then you probably fall into the second group, which is my case.

The page for my programme at Tallinn University asks for "background and/or previous experience in computer science, design, behavioral or social sciences."

*[on screen: the TLU HCI page, that line highlighted]*

So basically, when you see a programme you are interested in, try to put it into one of these three groups.

If it falls into group one or group two, that is perfect.

Even if it falls into group three, the one that asks for specific courses, sometimes there's still a door to get in.

### Build proof and sell your experience

If you're switching fields, the thing that really carries your application is proof that you can already do some of the work, especially if you are doing a master's degree.

My bachelor's degree is in chemistry, but I learned how to code, and I started working as a software developer in 2022.

By the time I was applying for my master's in 2025, I'd worked as a software developer and as a technical operations lead, and that work was my proof.

If you don't have work experience in the new field you're trying to move into, your proof can start smaller.

It can be a project that you build, finish and put online.

It can be a course where you did the assignments.

It can be volunteering, or running a community in that field.

But one thing I will always tell you is that you don't start building that proof at the point when you want to start applying.

Two months to the application, and you're just starting to volunteer? No.

You start building it long before the deadline, because you cannot build experience in the months before you apply.

If you have experience in the new field but your degree is in something else, how you describe that experience decides a lot.

If you have work experience like I do, you just have to sell your work and your technical experience well enough.

When I applied for my master's, I applied as someone with a technical background, even though my bachelor's degree certificate says chemistry.

And interestingly, with this same method, I also got into a computer science master's degree without a computer science bachelor's degree.

I intentionally declined that one, and I chose HCI instead.

*[your line, optional: one sentence on why, in your words; see Questions]*

And this works for job applications too, so stay with me if you are not applying for a master's.

Selling your experience starts with being specific.

Name your role, the tools you used, what you built, and what you fixed.

If you say things like "worked on the back end," that is too vague. Tell them what you did.

Then connect your experience to where you are going.

If you're a software developer and maybe you want to do an HCI master's degree, you build apps and you watch users struggle. That's a real link to a field like HCI.

Whatever experience you're trying to sell, you're selling it to the people making the decision in the new field.

So what I'll tell you is to write it the way the people in that field will read it. Use their words and their tools to communicate your experience.

### Your old degree comes with you

And remember those four questions for your motivation letter, they're coming right after this.

When you switch career fields, whatever you did in your bachelor's degree doesn't disappear. It comes with you.

When I was doing my bachelor's degree, I did a reasonable amount of research. I published two papers during my BSc.

So I had already gone through that process once, and that has made me more confident about writing my master's thesis.

My degree is in chemistry, and it trained me to be more analytical. I picked up one or two things from it that are still useful to me now.

Whatever your bachelor's degree is in, even if it's different from the master's you want to do, it has still trained you to do something.

If you have an accounting degree, it has trained you to be more exact with numbers than the average person.

Law trains you to read closely and argue a case.

Biology trains you to run experiments.

Now, I can't use my chemistry degree directly to talk my way into a master's in tech.

But I can use the skills I learned from it, and say clearly how they help me in the new field.

So make a list of what your degree has trained you to do, and use those words in your applications as well.

Your degree still opens doors for you. You just have to know how to communicate the skills it has given you.

### The motivation letter and the interview

*[printed letter + pen; black cards 1-4]*

If you're applying for a master's in a field that your bachelor's degree is not in, your motivation letter is where you explain your switch.

My advice is to sell your experience and your passion.

If you like the programme well enough, you won't find it hard to write.

And please be original. Write it yourself.

I feel like if you are making a career switch like that, your letter needs at least these four things.

Why this field? And why not the field you did your bachelor's degree in?

What have you already done in this field? Have you actually done something in it, or are you just fantasising about it?

Why this programme?

And what will you do with whatever you get from this programme?

*[on screen: 1. why this field, and why not your old one / 2. what you've already done in it / 3. why this programme / 4. what you'll do with it]*

Before you write your motivation letter, read what the department is working on. Read some of their papers, or at least the titles and abstracts.

I remember when I was applying for my programme, they even asked you to talk about your research interests, and what your thesis could be about.

And they could ask why someone with a degree in another field wants to do a master's in their programme.

Answer plainly. You don't have to apologise for your first degree. You did that, so own it.

*[say twice]*

Come with proof. Maybe you've started to build a passion for this new field, and you've started to get some experience in it.

But don't throw away your first degree, and don't talk down on it either.

This video isn't really about how to write motivation letters, but I would say, write your first draft and make it as long as possible.

Write everything that comes to your mind, and then you can start cutting it down to the main, important things.

If your master's application has an interview like mine, and your bachelor's degree was in another field, expect them to ask why you're switching.

For example, my bachelor's degree is in chemistry, and I'm moving into human-computer interaction.

Going into that interview, I should expect them to ask me why I'm switching.

So practise telling your story, right?

What you studied before, what you did after that, how you found your way into this field, and why you're planning to commit to this new field now.

*[on screen: what you studied / what you did after / how you found this field / why commit now]*

You have to have your answer ready before anybody asks you, because they probably will ask you.

### Give that programme a shot

*[setup 2]*

If you're about to switch fields with a degree in something else, and you want to do your master's in a field that is different from your bachelor's, give that programme a shot.

Even if you think your bachelor's degree might be a disadvantage, it might not be.

Don't let the title on your certificate decide for you before they've even turned you down.

*[say twice]*

So give it a shot.

Bachelor's degree in accounting, master's in, what can I say, go for it.

Bachelor's degree in law, master's degree in whatever, go for it.

Just go for it.

*[outro: record both, we use the one that fits]*

A: If you're thinking about doing your master's in Estonia, the next question is money. I made a whole video on what it actually costs to study here, and it's right here.

B: And if you're a Nigerian thinking about studying in Europe, watch this one next. It's everything nobody warned me about before I moved.

script:
### Open

I renewed my Nigerian passport from Estonia, where there's no Nigerian embassy, and I never left Tallinn.

*[on screen: top box "Renewing a Nigerian passport from abroad" · at "never left Tallinn" a small map card: Tallinn pin, Stockholm pin, dotted line, "0 trips"]*

This year, I renewed my Nigerian passport, because my passport expired some months ago.

So I had to do it through the Nigerian embassy in Stockholm, Sweden.

And I ended up using the contactless renewal option, so I didn't even leave Tallinn at all.

I'm gonna go over all the steps that I took in this video.

There's one button on the portal you shouldn't click first, and I'll show you which one when we get there.

And at the end I'll tell you what it all cost me, and the one thing I have not forgiven myself for.

Because honestly, it's a simple process, but if you're not careful, you just end up spending too long.

### Start early, because it takes time

The first step in renewing your Nigerian passport from abroad is the time.

*[on screen: step counter appears, top corner: STEP 1 / 9]*

Sometimes it just takes long.

But I think mine could have taken shorter if I had a proper overview of the process.

So you want to start trying to renew your passport at least two, three months before it expires, right?

I paid for mine in August, and it didn't get back to me until October.

Again, it could have taken a shorter time.

But it took too long because of some things I didn't do really well.

And I had to withdraw from a conference that I was paid to talk at, because my passport wasn't back in time.

So it's a very straightforward process.

And I'm going to show you every step, including the ones I didn't do well.

### Choose your processing embassy

When you renew your Nigerian passport from abroad, first things first, you have to choose a Nigerian embassy or high commission to process it.

*[on screen: step 2 / 9]*

You pick it on the application form.

I'll add the link to where you apply in the description.

So you choose your processing embassy.

You usually would want to choose somewhere close to you, right?

If the country you live in has a Nigerian embassy, then you don't have a problem.

You shouldn't even be watching this video, honestly.

Estonia doesn't have one.

On their website, the Stockholm embassy actually says they cover Denmark, Finland and Norway.

Estonia isn't on that list.

But my application went through regardless, and I know a few people here that did this through Sweden.

*[on screen: receipt card, Embassy of Nigeria Stockholm website: "Nigerian citizens residing in Sweden, Denmark, Finland, and Norway" (nigerianembassy.se, Nov 2026). Estonia isn't listed.]*

*[optional, only if you say yes to question 1]*
And for visas, their website says Estonia falls under the Nigerian embassy for Ukraine, which is in Vilnius right now, so you can ask them too.

So if your country isn't on their list, ask the embassy before you pay anything.

### Apply and pay on the NIS passport portal

To renew your Nigerian passport from abroad, you start on the Nigeria Immigration Service passport portal.

*[on screen: a generic portal screen with "Apply from outside Nigeria" circled]*

You choose the option for applying from outside Nigeria.

Then you choose renewal or reissue, whichever one you want.

You create your account.

You need your NIN, your National Identification Number, and you need your date of birth.

You fill the form, choose your processing embassy, upload your photo and your documents, and then you pay for the passport booklet.

As of October 2026, the Nigeria Immigration Service says the fees for Nigerians abroad are 150 dollars for a 32-page passport that lasts five years, and 230 dollars for the 64-page passport that lasts ten years.

*[on screen: receipt card, Voice of Nigeria 28 Aug 2025 quoting NIS: "remain unchanged at $150 for a 32-page passport ... and $230 for a 64-page passport" (unchanged as of Nov 2026)]*

So I chose the 64-page, ten-year one, and I paid 230 dollars.

### Your application ID and reference number

After you pay for your Nigerian passport on the NIS portal, you get an application ID and a reference number.

*[on screen: step 4 / 9]*

You have to keep that somewhere safe.

You will always see it on the dashboard, obviously, but just have it.

Whenever you contact the embassy, you definitely want to send your application number with it.

And also, only use the official NIS portal.

That's all you need.

### The passport photo problem

*[on screen: keep your Application ID and Reference Number safe / only use the official portal, passport.immigration.gov.ng]*

Problem number one for me was that the NIS passport portal kept rejecting my passport photo.

*[on screen: step 5 / 9, hold up the square photo]*

So you just keep trying until it goes through.

The first thing is the background.

Let your background colour be white.

The second one is the shape.

It has to kind of be like a portrait photo.

They didn't put so much detailed instruction, but at least the one that went through for me is a three by four shape, 600 by 800 pixels.

The square crops that I used got rejected.

*[hold up the portrait photo]*

And also the size of your head, your face.

Your face has to fill like 70 to 80 percent of the height of the photo, and sit at the centre.

*[on screen: what finally went through for me: white background / portrait, 3 by 4, 600 x 800 pixels / face about 70 to 80% of the height, centred]*

So I'd tell you to reshoot your photo against a white wall from the start, and save yourself the back and forth.

### Contactless biometric enrolment in the NIS mobile app

The reason why I never went to Stockholm in person was because I used the contactless renewal option.

*[on screen: step 6 / 9]*

It's called contactless biometric enrolment.

It means that you capture your face and your fingerprints in the NIS Mobile app, on a phone, rather than at the embassy.

It was announced for Nigerians in Europe in February 2025.

I think it started in Canada first, and then the UK and Ireland.

But it doesn't cover first-time applicants or children.

*[on screen: receipt card, Federal Ministry of Interior, 7 Feb 2025: "eligible Nigerians in Europe can renew their passports entirely online" · small line: Canada first (Nov 2024), then the UK and Ireland; renewals only (news reports at the launch)]*

And this is the button I told you about.

After you've paid for the booklet, the contactless option will show up on your application status page.

*[phone inset: generic "Application status" screen, "Opt-In for Contactless" circled green, "Book appointment" crossed red]*

And it's different from the appointment calendar.

If you go into the appointment calendar first, it can lock you into the in-person route.

*[say twice]*

And you don't want to go in person, right?

I didn't want to go in person.

*[on screen: after you pay, look on Application Status for the contactless option. Don't open the appointment calendar first.]*

And the fingerprint part is the one that gave me trouble, so stay with me.

So from there, you download the NIS Mobile app, you open Passport Biometric Enrolment, and you enter your application ID and reference number.

The app will check if you're eligible.

If you're eligible, you capture your face.

It checks if there's a live person in front of the camera.

That was very easy.

It was the fingerprint that was hard for me.

I think I spent about an hour back and forth with the fingerprint one.

You press your fingerprint, and then it gives you a quality score.

That one gave me a lot of back and forth, personally, but it wasn't even up to one hour.

But I kept trying, trying, trying, and I didn't give up.

So I paid 100 dollars for this contactless thingy.

Check the amount in the app when you get there.

*[on screen: in the app: Application ID + Reference Number / eligibility check / face + liveness / fingerprints, each with a quality score / contactless fee (I paid $100)]*

When I did mine, the NIS Mobile app was not on the iPhone App Store in Estonia, so I had to borrow an Android phone.

They now have an iPhone version, but it's still not on the Estonian App Store, so check if it's in your country.

By the way, if you're in the app and it says that you're not eligible for contactless, then go back to the portal and book an in-person appointment instead.

### The embassy admin fee, and contacting the embassy

After the contactless enrolment, you pay the embassy admin fee for your Nigerian passport renewal.

*[on screen: step 7 / 9]*

You pay it straight to the embassy. They have an account.

The one in Stockholm was 500 Swedish kronor, and it's non-refundable.

So you pay, and of course, check the website.

It could have increased or decreased by the time you're watching this video.

And I think when I paid, I even reached out to them for confirmation, and they confirmed.

*[on screen: receipt card, Stockholm embassy passport page (Nov 2026): "500 SEK administrative fee ... 3-6 weeks processing". Each embassy sets its own, so check its official page and pay only to the account listed there.]*

And there's also a phone number that I would call from time to time.

But what I noticed is that whenever you want to email the embassy, email them with your application number, and keep your message short.

### When a document gets queried

While you're doing all of this, your Nigerian passport application is being processed at the same time, and it can get queried.

*[on screen: step 8 / 9]*

Any document on your application can get queried.

For example, in my case, my birth certificate got queried.

So I had to replace it with a sworn affidavit of age before my application got vetted.

### Sending your old passport and a return label

*[on screen: my application: birth certificate queried, replaced with a sworn affidavit of age, then the status showed Vetted]*

Even with contactless biometrics, you still have to send your old Nigerian passport to the embassy.

*[on screen: step 9 / 9]*

If you don't send your old passport, they may not issue your new one.

So I sent a package to the embassy with my old passport, my printed application form, the receipts of the payments I had made, and a prepaid return label.

The return label is because the embassy also has to send your new passport back to you.

The Stockholm embassy only accepts DHL and UPS.

DHL is super expensive.

I hate that I used DHL.

I used DHL when I was sending, and I used UPS for the return.

And it takes about three weeks-ish once the embassy gets it.

### Delivery, and what it all cost me

*[on screen: what I sent: old passport / printed application form / payment receipts / prepaid return label. Stockholm: DHL or UPS only. You can track it after two weeks at track.immigration.gov.ng.]*

From paying in August, I got my new Nigerian passport delivered to me on the 8th of October, and I never left Tallinn.

So, what did it all cost me?

So, 230 dollars for the passport, 100 dollars for the contactless enrolment, and 500 Swedish kronor for the embassy fee.

And of course, the money you use to send the packages back and forth.

I think everything came to about 424 euros.

*[say twice]*

*[on screen: receipt card building line by line: $230 passport (64 pages, 10 years) + $100 contactless + 500 SEK embassy fee + couriers = about €424 (Aug to Oct 2026)]*

I paid for DHL when I was sending it, and I regret it, because I should have just used UPS, which would have cost me maybe 20-something or 30 euros.

So I have not forgiven myself for that.

A: And if you're studying abroad and working at the same time, I made a video on how I work full time while doing my master's here in Estonia. It's right here.
B: And if you're a Nigerian thinking about studying in Europe, watch the video I made on everything nobody warned me about. It's right here.

script:
### Paystack vs Flutterwave

Say you're building an app in Nigeria and you want people to pay you online. You'll most likely choose between Paystack and Flutterwave.

And the cheaper one changes with the size of your order. There's even one order size where both of them charge exactly the same fee, and I'll show you that number.

In this video, I'm comparing the two using their official pricing pages and documentation, as of November 2026.

We'll go through what they charge, how fast you get paid, how to sign up and how to build with each one, and then which one I would pick for which kind of app.

And if you're a developer, stay for the code part, because the integration is almost the same on both.

*[on screen: "PAYSTACK or FLUTTERWAVE?" / then the empty comparison table: rows "local fee · cap · cheaper for · international · countries · payout · transfers · no CAC? · webhook"]*

Paystack and Flutterwave are payment gateways.

A payment gateway sits between your app and your customer's bank.

So if I have a cute dresses app, and someone is buying a dress for 100,000 naira, my app sends them to Paystack's or Flutterwave's checkout.

The gateway collects the money, tells my app that the payment worked, and later sends the money to my bank account.

It removes its own fee before the money gets to that bank account.

*[prop: your phone, showing a checkout]*

*[on screen: customer pays on the checkout / gateway tells your app / money reaches your bank, minus the fee]*

Now, like I said, these payment gateways also take their own fees.

### What each one charges

These are Paystack's fees for a business in Nigeria, from their pricing page as of November 2026.

For local payments, Paystack charges 1.5% plus 100 naira, whether your customer paid with a card, a bank transfer or USSD.

If the payment is under 2,500 naira, Paystack waives the 100 naira, and you only pay the 1.5%.

And the fee is capped at 2,000 naira.

So whether somebody pays 200,000 naira or 2 million naira, the local fee is 2,000 naira.

For international cards, it's 3.9% plus 100 naira, and American Express cards are 4.5%.

*[on screen: Paystack Nigeria, Nov 2026 / local: 1.5% + ₦100 / ₦100 waived under ₦2,500 / capped at ₦2,000 / international cards: 3.9% + ₦100 / Amex: 4.5%; screenshot of the pricing page with the cap highlighted. Table row "local fee" + "cap" fill for Paystack]*

Now, these are Flutterwave's fees for a business in Nigeria, also from their pricing page as of November 2026.

For local payments, Flutterwave charges 2%, which they split into a 1.4% transaction fee and a 0.6% platform fee.

Flutterwave's pricing page doesn't list a maximum fee for local payments, so a bigger payment means a bigger fee.

For international payments, it's 4.8%, and the page says the fees are subject to 7.5% VAT.

*[on screen: Flutterwave Nigeria, Nov 2026 / local: 2% (1.4% + 0.6%) / no maximum fee listed / international: 4.8% / fees subject to 7.5% VAT; screenshot of the page. Table rows fill for Flutterwave]*

On Flutterwave, your customer pays the fee by default, on top of your price, and you can change that.

On Paystack, passing the fee to your customer is a setting you turn on.

### The same order on both

Now, which one is cheaper, Paystack or Flutterwave?

It depends on the size of the order, so let's run the same pretty dress orders through both.

I'm using their listed prices and leaving VAT out for both, so we are comparing like with like.

A 2,000 naira order.

Paystack waives the 100 naira, so the fee is 30 naira.

Flutterwave's fee in this case will be 40 naira.

A 10,000 naira order.

Paystack's fee is 250 naira.

Flutterwave's fee is 200 naira.

And this is the number I promised you. At 20,000 naira, both of them charge exactly 400 naira.

For a 50,000 naira order, Paystack's fee is 850 naira, while Flutterwave's is 1,000 naira.

For a 200,000 naira order, Paystack's fee is capped, so it's 2,000 naira, while Flutterwave's is 4,000 naira.

*[on screen: table / order: ₦2,000 · ₦10,000 · ₦20,000 · ₦50,000 · ₦200,000 / Paystack: ₦30 · ₦250 · ₦400 · ₦850 · ₦2,000 / Flutterwave: ₦40 · ₦200 · ₦400 · ₦1,000 · ₦4,000 / listed prices, before VAT, Nov 2026. Then the two-line chart crossing at ₦20,000 (same picture as thumbnail E)]*

So on listed prices, Flutterwave is a little cheaper for orders between 2,500 and 20,000 naira.

Paystack is cheaper under 2,500 and above 20,000, and the gap grows as the order gets bigger.

And also, with Paystack, if you process a lot of money, their pricing page says you can get a volume discount on the fee.

### Selling outside Nigeria and getting paid

*[check 0g first; cut this line if the page no longer says it]*

*[Table row "cheaper for" fills: Paystack "under ₦2,500 and above ₦20,000" / Flutterwave "₦2,500 to ₦20,000"]*

If you are selling outside Nigeria and using Paystack or Flutterwave, there are also some things to consider.

Paystack's services are available to businesses registered in Nigeria, Ghana, South Africa and Kenya, with a private beta in Côte d'Ivoire and Egypt.

Flutterwave's pricing page has 12 African countries, including Uganda, Tanzania, Rwanda and Senegal.

*[on screen: two simple Africa maps, 4 countries (+2 beta) vs 12 countries]*

For international cards, Paystack charges 3.9% plus 100 naira, while Flutterwave charges 4.8%.

By default, both of them settle the payment to a Nigerian business in naira.

Now, Paystack lets you choose to be settled in dollars instead, into a Zenith Bank domiciliary account.

*[no "pilot" label unless the pricing page still says it]*

*[on screen: Paystack USD settlement into a Zenith Bank domiciliary account]*

Now, how fast do Paystack and Flutterwave pay you?

Once a customer pays, how fast does the money reach your account?

Paystack's pricing page says the next working day, so Monday's payments will arrive on Tuesday.

Flutterwave's pricing page says the next day for local payments, and international payments vary by region.

*[on screen: Paystack: next working day (T+1) / Flutterwave: next day for local, international varies by region]*

If you're paying out from your account, like, for example, maybe you are paying a designer whose dresses you sell on your own platform, Paystack and Flutterwave charge the same transfer fees.

It's 10 naira for 5,000 and below, 25 naira for up to 50,000, and 50 naira above that.

### Signing up without CAC

*[on screen: transfers in Nigeria, both: ₦10 (₦5,000 and below) / ₦25 (₦5,001 to ₦50,000) / ₦50 (above ₦50,000) / Flutterwave adds 7.5% VAT]*

If you're a Nigerian business setting up online payments, do you need to register with CAC before you can accept payments with Flutterwave or Paystack?

Actually, on both, you can start as an unregistered business.

On Paystack, it's called a Starter Business.

You sign up with your government ID, your BVN and your personal bank account, all in the same name.

And a Starter Business can take up to 8 million naira, but it can't send transfers.

To remove those limits, you have to upgrade to a Registered Business with your CAC documents.

With Flutterwave, the starter option asks for your BVN, your NIN, an ID, proof of address, a website or social media page, and your estimated monthly sales.

### How the integration works

*[on screen: Paystack Starter: ID + BVN + personal bank account, same name / up to ₦8m, no transfers / Flutterwave starter: BVN + NIN, ID, proof of address, website or social page, estimated monthly sales / Registered on both: CAC documents]*

If you're a developer, Paystack and Flutterwave kind of work the same way, in four steps.

First, your server starts the payment with your secret key and gets back a checkout link.

Second, your customer pays on that checkout, and they are sent back to your site.

Third, your server asks the payment gateway if the payment went through, and checks the status and the amount before marking the order as paid.

And fourth, the gateway also tells your server directly that the payment went through, with something called a webhook.

*[on screen: 1. start the payment / 2. customer pays / 3. verify on your server / 4. webhook]*

*[on screen: screen recording in a big window beside you; you stay in frame]*
```php
// If you're using Laravel, for example

// Paystack: start the payment, then verify
Http::withToken($paystackSecret)->post('https://api.paystack.co/transaction/initialize', [
    'email'  => $order->email,
    'amount' => $order->total * 100, // kobo
]);

Http::withToken($paystackSecret)
    ->get("https://api.paystack.co/transaction/verify/{$reference}");
// paid only if data.status is "success" and the amount matches

// Flutterwave Standard (v3): start the payment, then verify
Http::withToken($flutterwaveSecret)->post('https://api.flutterwave.com/v3/payments', [
    'tx_ref'       => $order->reference,
    'amount'       => $order->total,
    'currency'     => 'NGN',
    'redirect_url' => route('payment.callback'),
    'customer'     => ['email' => $order->email],
]);

Http::withToken($flutterwaveSecret)
    ->get("https://api.flutterwave.com/v3/transactions/{$transactionId}/verify");
// paid only if data.status is "successful" and the amount and currency match
```

For webhooks, Paystack signs each one with your secret key in a header called x-paystack-signature.

Flutterwave sends the secret hash you set in your dashboard, in a header called verif-hash.

On both of them, you check that header before you trust the webhook, and you send back a 200.

```php
// Paystack
$valid = hash_equals(
    hash_hmac('sha512', $request->getContent(), $paystackSecret),
    (string) $request->header('x-paystack-signature')
);

// Flutterwave
$valid = hash_equals($flutterwaveSecretHash, (string) $request->header('verif-hash'));
```

### Which one should you use?

So which one should you use, Paystack or Flutterwave?

This is how I would decide.

If you sell in Nigeria and your orders are usually above 20,000 naira, like courses or electronics, I'd lean a little bit towards Paystack, because of the lower percentage and the 2,000 naira cap.

If most of your orders are between 2,500 and 20,000 naira, like books or food, Flutterwave's listed price comes out a little cheaper.

If you want your business live in more African countries, I'd look at Flutterwave first.

If you haven't registered with CAC, yes, both of them let you start, but Paystack has an 8 million naira Starter limit.

If payments are your whole business, I think it's worth setting up both, so on a bad day, your company is not stuck with one provider.

*[on screen: the full comparison table, every row filled, the "your order size" row highlighted]*

*[outro: record both, we use the one that fits]*

A: If you've picked Paystack and you want to see it working in a real app, I have a full tutorial where I add Paystack to a Next.js app, step by step. It's right here. And I'm making one for Laravel too.

B: If you're building with Laravel, I made a full video on adding Paystack payments to a Laravel app, from the first request to the webhook. That's the one to watch next.
